item.title: Surviving the Messy Middle: Finding Hope When Life Doesn’t Follow the Timeline You Expected
item.description:
Have you ever looked around and wondered why everyone else’s life seems to be moving forward while yours feels stuck? Any delay in the gratification of something we have been working for can be amplified to excruciating disappointment, frustration, and pain in this modern era of watching family and friends’ highlight reels on social media.

There is ample opportunity to find “evidence” that you have missed the mark or worse, that something might be wrong with you. The messy middle can be a tough time for many, especially when outcomes don’t match the timelines we hoped for.

Life is often hardest, not at the beginning or end of a journey, but in the middle, where the outcome is still unknown. This transitional period is not a sign that something is wrong, but that you are actually normal. Although it may be difficult, it is indeed survivable and a place where formation and transformation can occur.

Why the Middle Feels So Hard

There are many ways to prepare yourself for the beginning or end of milestones, but few people teach us how to live between them. This is the season in between. When you are standing in between what once was and what you hoped would happen, with a current reality that is different. The couple who excitedly set out to conceive a child only to receive a diagnosis of infertility experience a plan much different than the original.

You get laid off from the job you were comfortable with and now find yourself one of hundreds of applicants for one position with no guaranteed outcome. Whether you are overcoming burnout, in the middle of parenting struggles, or coping with aging parents, you are different from where you started, and the end may feel uncertain.

One simple way to think about this is that change is what happens to you; transition is what happens inside of you. The change often happens quickly, but your heart and mind are still trying to catch up. We may feel frustrated that things aren’t moving along more quickly and can question whether God is even listening to our prayers at this point. The truth is that people adapt to external change much more slowly than they expect.

Why Uncertainty Feels So Emotionally Exhausting

Our brain experiences waiting and ambiguity as a threat to our nervous system instead of something more neutral. We are wired to predict outcomes, and when uncertainty arises, our brains will search for outcomes to relieve the discomfort.

When we’ve had an extended season of waiting, we can begin to see negative thoughts and feelings present themselves. We can imagine a loyal guard dog living inside our chest whose main job is to keep us safe. When something feels safe, he lies down. When something makes him feel threatened, he barks, but he’s never been trained for the third option of not knowing.

So, when you are in the thick of waiting, between the old job and the new one, between diagnosis and the answer, between who you used to be and who you are becoming, your guard dog doesn’t experience the silence as peace. It experiences it more like “something bad is coming, and I don’t know what it is.” He doesn’t know what to do with it, so he barks.

In a prolonged waiting season, you may experience racing thoughts, difficulty sleeping, irritability, anger, muscle tension, difficulty concentrating, and emotional exhaustion. The Bible gives us a relatable example when the Psalmist writes:

O Lord, how long will you forget me? Forever? How long will you look the other way? How long must I struggle with anguish in my soul, with sorrow in my heart every day? How long will my enemy have the upper hand? – Psalms 13:1-2, NLT

This isn’t a sign of being weak or a sign that you have a lack of faith. You are not overacting. Your nervous system just hasn’t learned yet that you are safe, and it can calm down.

When Reality Doesn’t Match Our Timeline

Whether we realize it or not, most of us have a quiet image of how we thought our lives would go. Most of us are flexible with exactly how or when we achieve the image of our futures, but we have milestones in our mind that we’d like to meet. When life takes its twists and turns, we can be blindsided by the grief we experience.

We expect grief in obvious circumstances of death and loss, but we are often not prepared for the grief that occurs when the dreams we hoped for don’t go as planned:

  • The woman who thought she would be a mother in her twenties.
  • The professional who thought the promotion would finally provide the fulfillment they’ve been anticipating.
  • The couple who thought they would spend their lives together.
  • The college student who thought they would have a lucrative career after graduation.

These losses are not always visible to the world around us, but they impact us, nonetheless. When the loss is not tangible, we can judge ourselves for experiencing grief.

Our timelines become unexpected contracts by which we measure our personal success. It is healthy and natural to have goals and dreams for our future. The challenge is that often there are things outside of our control that impact how our timelines unfold. When we begin to attach our peace to specific outcomes and dates, we set a trap that turns an event into evidence of our self-inadequacy.

The disappointment builds resentment and bitterness, and we can find ourselves trapped in a negative spiral, asking, “Did I do something wrong to deserve this? Did I miss God’s will, and am I being punished? Will my life always look like this?” This only further increases our emotional suffering. We compare ourselves to friends, family, and colleagues who seemingly have it together, and we may begin to fear that it will never change.

This can be a critical emotional turning point in our lives. We begin to misinterpret the emotions that we are feeling, which can create more distress. We begin to see ourselves as weak, failing, too emotional, or not trusting God enough. Instead of seeing the sadness as possible grief or the emotional exhaustion as the result of carrying a burden we weren’t meant to carry.

It is important to accurately label emotions so that we can reduce the burden of shame and create space for healing. Acceptance of your experience can feel like total defeat and abandonment of all hope. The reality is that acceptance can give us a snapshot of where we actually are today so we can respond wisely, rather than staying stuck in a reality we cannot change. The goal isn’t to try to force the timeline to move faster, but to stay grounded and present, and to wait.

Growth happens in the waiting, not just the arrival

There is no magical wand that we can wave and rush forward to the outcomes we desire. However, we can teach the nervous system that it doesn’t have to remain braced for impact while we are waiting. The goal for these tools is not to end the uncertainty, but to help your body and mind to find rest while you are in it. Here are a few that can help.

The Physiological Sigh

Short, shallow breaths do not signal to the body that it is safe. However, when we slow our breathing, our body begins to relax, and we may notice our thoughts slow down as well. A double inhale through the nose (one long inhale and one short inhale on top of it), followed by a long exhale through the mouth, will begin to signal to the body that it is safe.

Try this: The next time you find your mind racing, stop and take three physiological sighs before you try to think your way through it. Let your body settle down first.

Naming the Tension

Uncertainty often reveals itself in our bodies long before we can catch it cognitively. A tight jaw, teeth grinding, tightness in our chest, clenched bellies, or shoulders creeping up toward your ears may be the symptoms we notice before our thoughts start spiraling.

Try this: Once a day, pause and ask where you are holding tension in your body right now. Simply naming the places where you feel tension, without trying to fix it, will naturally help the grip loosen.

Movement as Release

Stress hormones are meant to move through our bodies; however, when we are experiencing tension, we can unintentionally trap them. Going for a short walk, stretching, shaking your hands, or heel drops can create movement so that you can discharge what’s built up from being on alert.

Try this: Go on a five-minute walk, if possible, with your phone left behind at the time of day when worry tends to feel the loudest.

Breath Prayer

This is where the body and faith meet. Choose a scripture or short phrase and pray it rhythmically with your breath. Breathe in the first part of the prayer, exhale the second half.

Try this: Inhale “Be still,” exhale “and know.” (Psalm 46:10) Use this anywhere, in the car, at your desk, in bed, mid-spiral. It’s a way to tell your body the truth that you are safe and not alone in this when your emotions and thoughts have not quite caught up.

None of these exercises will make the waiting end sooner. But, with practice, each step moves your body closer to rest while you are walking through transition, even before you have all the answers. It’s not giving up or resigning to failure but allowing space to make your best choices from true peace.

Reframing Discomfort as Formation

Almost no one enjoys the messy middle of waiting, but almost everyone will be marked one way or another by this experience. We always have a choice; we can stay stuck in the waiting, angry, resentful, or bitter, or we can allow it to form something beautiful in us. When we allow the waiting to reveal the parts in us that need healing, we can move through this season healthier than when we entered it.

The Bible tells us that there are opportunities for growth and endurance to be built in challenges we experience (James 1:2-4; Romans 5:3-5). It’s not because God has it in for you, or that you are being punished, but that the opportunity can lead to greater inner healing and a greater relationship with God.

Your life is valuable no matter what the outcome of a waiting season may be. This can feel daunting in the middle, and you may find that you need support as you learn to feel steady.

You don’t have to wait alone

The messy middle doesn’t ask for your permission before it arrives and rarely leaves on the timeline you would like it to. You don’t have to white-knuckle your way through it or attempt to create movement with sheer willpower.

Learning to breathe more effectively, notice where you are holding tension, move your body, or pray honestly, instead of performing peace, are little ways to manage the tough days one by one. They are little reassurances to your body, reinforcing the truth that you are being held, even in the middle.

If you are in a season where the waiting is starting to wear on you, help is available. Our counselors would be honored to walk alongside you, offering practical tools to support you in this season. You were never meant to carry this burden on your own. Reach out to schedule a session with one of the counselors when you are ready.

And I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ. – Philippians 1:6, ESV

item.title: How Jealousy Can Become Part of the Grieving Process
item.description:
Many people have been taught that grief happens in stages, culminating in acceptance as a final stage. However, grief is far more complex, difficult, and unpredictable. It affects people in ways they might never have expected.

Although so few people talk about it, one of the most common aspects of the grieving process is jealousy. It is common for people to experience intense jealousy as they grieve, especially when they are reminded of all the precious and meaningful things that they have lost. Understanding why you are feeling jealousy as you grieve is an important part of coping, healing, and adapting to your life after the loss of a loved one.

The Injustice of Death

Everyone knows that death is inevitable, but when it comes, it always feels sudden, overwhelming, and unfair. There will be days when you remember your lost loved one fondly and even humorously, and days when you are consumed with regret, anger, and hopelessness. The dull ache of their absence is only made worse by the constant reminders that life simply goes on.

Your entire world might have crumbled when they died, but everyone else continued their lives oblivious to your pain. Not only that, but at some point, you were uncomfortably reminded that other people have what you are now missing.

There are many triggers to grief, and many reminders that death is sudden and unfair. Important dates, birthdays, holidays, and anniversaries are some of the most difficult times to navigate as a griever because they serve as stark reminders of all you now miss. Everywhere you look, you see people who still have their loved ones and lives that went unchanged.

What Jealousy in Grief Looks Like

You might never have been a jealous person until you began grieving. Now there are constant reminders of what you have lost that other people still have. Not many people share this particular part of the grieving process because they feel guilt, shame, or embarrassment over feeling jealous in their grief. However, when you consider some of the contexts of their jealousy, it makes sense that they should feel this way.

Jealousy in grief might look like:

  • Being jealous of the relationships siblings have with each other when you have lost your sibling
  • Being jealous of the survivors of an accident that claimed your loved one
  • Being jealous of friends, family, or coworkers who have never experienced loss like you have
  • Being jealous of happy families, especially during the holidays
  • Being jealous of people in happy marriages after losing your spouse
  • Being jealous of parents after losing your child
  • Being jealous of healthy pregnant women after a miscarriage
  • Being jealous of how others are supported in their grief when you feel alone in yours

Jealousy, on its own, is a complex emotion. It feels like a combination of anger, sadness, hatred, dissatisfaction, and emptiness. When you acknowledge your feelings of jealousy and begin peeling back the layers of emotions you feel, you will soon realize that, at its core, jealousy is about having unmet needs. That’s when it begins to make sense that jealousy is a common part of the grieving process; you have deep unmet needs as someone who has lost a loved one.

The Impact of Social Media on the Grieving Process

Grief is exhausting in every way, even physically. At some point in the grieving process, it is normal to seek out lighthearted distractions and fun interactions with others. Social media often feels like the perfect escape and distraction for times when things have become too intense and heavy.

With just a few scrolls on your phone, you can find humor, entertainment, conversation, and news on everything that is happening outside of your experience. However, this often comes with the caveat of seeing things that trigger your jealousy, frustration, and longing. It’s not that you want what others currently have. It is often a longing for the things you once had. That difference is important.

You are not a bad person for feeling intense jealousy over someone else’s life. You are also not a bad person for sometimes wishing that they could feel what you now feel. These thoughts and emotions show that you are lonely, that you are longing, that you have a hurt that can’t be easily healed, and a love that can’t easily be forgotten. You are not a bad person for feeling jealousy in grief; you are human with a broken heart, and there is a lot of grace for you.

Coping with Jealousy in Grief

Like many things in life, the best way to cope with jealousy in grief is to acknowledge it. It is simply a natural part of grief for many people, and not an indicator that something is wrong with you. You might be making your jealousy worse by dwelling on it or continuing to scroll the social media accounts you find triggering, but you are not to blame ultimately. Truthfully, no one is to blame.

One of the best things you can do as you grieve is to give yourself and others a break. For a while, you won’t have the same capacity you once did for even simple daily tasks. A lot of your mental bandwidth is now taken up by complex emotions and a survival instinct.

Similarly, people are not trying to provoke you to jealousy or anger as you grieve. They might be self-absorbed or tactless, but if they knew your emotional state, they would likely want to help if they could. That is especially true for your family, friends, and loved ones.

Remind yourself that this isn’t your new normal. Grief is messy and complex, and some people get stuck in it, but your emotions will calibrate, and your life will adjust. Time doesn’t heal all wounds, but you do begin to learn new methods of coping and new ways of communicating. If you are not okay now, that is okay. One day, you will be okay again.

Painted Memories

In her book series beginning with The Hunger Games, Suzanne Collins explores grief in a variety of vivid, helpful ways in the context of a young adult dystopian story. The characters in the book series have all been affected by loss and injustice to varying degrees, and many struggle to cope.

Two characters find one of the most helpful and beautiful methods of coping with the loss of so many loved ones. In a large book, one of them begins painting portraits of the people they have lost, while the other writes down notes on their character, like what their favorite things were and what they were most well-known for. This book becomes their primary way of holding all the pain, loss, and love together without forgetting the ones they lost.

The grieving process is something that no one heals from, and it doesn’t happen in neat stages. You will feel a variety of intense emotions at some point, and at other times you will feel numb to everything. You will worry that the memory of your loved one is fading, and at another point, you will dream vividly of them, as if they were still alive.

No one can tell you what to feel or how to cope, but you can find help if you feel stuck in grief. Cherish the memory of your loved one, and remember that you are not alone in whatever emotions you go through in grief.

If you would like to find a counselor to help you through the grieving process or a support group to attend, please get in touch with us. You might find help in our online catalog of counselors, or you can contact our reception team. We hope that you can find the support you need.

item.title: Managing Attention and Hyperactivity Deficits with Counseling
item.description:
Attention deficit and hyperactivity disorder, where a person has difficulty concentrating to the point of completing tasks, or impulsivity, a type of driven restlessness to a degree that it impacts all areas of life, is not a newly noted pattern in human behavior.

The description has shown up in literature in different ways throughout recent history, and most likely will change again over time as more is discovered about where it comes from and how it appears or presents itself in cultures over time (Lange K.W. Et al., 2010). There certainly has been a lot of progress in tracking and understanding the description of behaviors.

There are also now numerous, effective, researched ways to understand and manage the symptoms, all of which should be, when in relationship with God, wrestled with and considered before Him. Understanding can begin by meeting with your doctor or a psychologist or therapist to assess whether your symptoms meet the criteria for the diagnosis.

Then, as with all things in making decisions, including mental health diagnosis and its treatment, we are invited to pray, review Scripture for guidance, and seek wise counsel to learn to manage ourselves.

In the written encouragement from E. Welch (2024), “The most important principle is that your quest for medical treatment does not outdistance your diligence in spiritual nurture.” Counseling with a mental health professional, grounded in Christ and biblical truths, can be one way to explore and develop understanding and skills to manage ADHD.

What is ADHD?

Before describing ADHD, there needs to be a discussion of the importance of the descriptors themselves. Frustration has been expressed at the ways in which terms for the same behavior or descriptors change over time. Does what we call something really matter? The pendulum may swing, but we must let it land where the Lord directs. We are directed to be thoughtful of how our words affect others.

As Proverbs 18:21 (CSB) says, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue….” Additionally, we are directed to be mindful of what we say, as it reflects our hearts, and mindful of how our words will impact others and the situations we are in (cf. Proverbs 10:19).

Additionally, the euphemism, “I just don’t have the words,” exists for a reason. Language can fall short of describing what we see and know. Ultimately, what we say matters in our own heads to ourselves and toward others. Bearing that in mind, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is one description of a set of patterns of behaviors. It is not a newly recognized nuance in human behavior.

Descriptions of inattention first appeared in literature in 1798 by Sir Alexander Crichton, where he explored what might be typical versus atypical patterns of attention (Lange K.W. Et al., 2010). Centuries later, ADHD is described by the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (DSM-5-TR) as a combination of six or more specific symptoms of inattention or hyperactivity, or both.

They must be present for more than six months, having started before the age of twelve, and significantly impact more than two areas of life in ways that negatively impact the person and are not consistent with what are considered developmental averages.

What medical or mental health providers are looking for is how attention and activity show up and impact living. Consider that a person with attention-deficit can attend and concentrate highly on a singular task, usually something of great interest to them, which is usually not the task at hand or required in their setting.

Attention is rapidly pulled to multiple places, like someone changing the TV channel multiple times without consent (Copeland and Dumm, 2015). It is physiologically and often emotionally exhausting, and this is where behavior starts to affect functioning in different settings.

Nowell, David, Ph.D. (2019) calls this “The GAP.” Hyperactivity is a type of driven restlessness, like an overheated internal motor that is either set to max RPMs at all times, looking for ways to release the vibrating energy, or turned completely off. ADHD is essentially not about a person’s ability, but a person’s performance.

When diagnosing ADHD, it is important that symptoms are differentiated from what is simply healthy play or activities for children and adults. An assessment also should consider a person’s personality, their environment, stressors, and medical implications that may present like ADHD, but are not actually its cause.

ADHD needs to be assessed, and other diagnoses that impact cognition and brain functioning need to be considered; things like learning disabilities, possible traumatic brain injuries, substances, etc. (Welch, 2024).

Where ADHD Comes From

There is still much to learn about ADHD and its development. Even research appears to disagree with itself, where some studies state that there is no concrete evidence that ADHD brain development and functioning are different from other neurotypical brains (Welch, 2024). Other research points to evidence that there is indeed neurodivergence in someone who has ADHD (Nowell, David, Ph.D. (2019, February).

What is known is that some factors increase the likelihood of ADHD behaviors recurring, such as heritability (where parents had the official diagnosis or presented with similar behaviors), children with low birth weight, infants and children exposed to nicotine and alcohol, and chemical changes that occur from extreme stress occurring from different factors in parents.

Studies of people with an ADHD diagnosis show a thinner cortex, more activity in the occipital lobe, the back of the brain, which impacts visual learning, and less activity in the frontal and temporal lobes where sequencing and decision-making occur (Nowell, David, Ph.D. (2019, February).

When is it really inattention and hyperactivity disorder?

As every person has their own unique summary of genetics and experiences, ADHD may look different in how it shows up from day to day. Therefore, it is essential that when managing ADHD, diagnosing ADHD, or relating to someone with ADHD, you get to know yourself or that person to figure out where the performance GAPS exist and why, and over time. Again, ADHD is not about a person’s intelligence; it is about performance.

The criteria for assessment are important in this, assessing the way symptoms show up across different environments and from a young age. For example, a parent expresses their concern that their child will make eye contact briefly but then act as if the connection was not made and begin behaving beyond or outside of what they were requested to do. This may fall under the category of difficulty sustaining attention.

In order to assess whether this is part of ADHD, an assessment needs to evaluate multiple factors to identify why this behavior occurs in daily life. Questions should be explored, such as whether the child may have hearing or vision impairment that may be impacting connection.

Is there a cultural layer at play where direct or sustained eye contact with a parent is acceptable? When, where, and how is the child being required to provide sustained attention? Is the environment chaotic or peaceful in these contexts? Is the concern only happening with one parent, or with all people? Is the child’s personality assertive or more passive? Did the child just eat, and maybe mood fluctuation is playing a role?

There are many ways and reasons divergence appears in daily life, but what is imperative is careful and thoughtful consideration of why it is impacting progress or daily functioning.

Using Counseling to Manage ADHD

As noted previously, the first step to diagnosing and managing ADHD is to pray about it. Set a rhythm of bringing thoughts and curiosities to God and anticipating that He will respond in expected and unexpected ways. This may be through Scripture, through exploration of literature on the subject, through others with wise advice and encouragement, and through counseling.

In addition, consider scheduling multiple appointments to meet with a primary care physician, a psychologist, and a therapist to have symptoms assessed. Consider their feedback and whether there is a pattern that illuminates what might be occurring. Ongoing counseling, regardless of the outcomes from a doctor and psychologist, can be beneficial in addressing what problems may be arising that led to an assessment of symptoms in the first place.

A counselor can help be a resource or director of increasing self-awareness and education about symptoms. They could provide literature and self-help tools to begin managing symptoms. Counselors can adjust session times, styles, and treatment interventions to help develop self-management tools and skills.

For some people with ADHD, medication is part of their management tools, and counseling can be a good place to process the feelings and integration of medication after seeing their doctor or psychiatrist for the actual prescription of medication. A counselor can become the one person who works to understand their experience, identify the differences in their experience, provide direction, and walk alongside with compassion.

Lastly, a counselor rooted in Christ and biblical faith can help illuminate how to practically implement God’s encouragement to all of us to have rhythms that reflect him, or filter life through Christ, no matter how our brains operate or our bodies move.

item.title: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) for Treating Major Depressive Disorders
item.description:
All human beings experience negative or sad moods at times. However, if these or other symptoms are making it hard to function, you may be suffering from clinical depression. A clinical diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) requires five or more symptoms over the same two-week period, including either a depressed mood or loss of interest or pleasure, plus significant distress, or impaired functioning.

Although not a complete list, symptoms may include agitation, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt, problems with thinking, concentrating, or making decisions, recurring thoughts of death, suicidal thoughts, or suicide attempts.

These symptoms are a change from prior functioning and are not due to another medical condition or substance use. Whether or not you meet the full clinical criteria, seeking out therapy is appropriate if you are experiencing symptoms that distress you or limit your full engagement in life.

Medication for Major Depressive Disorders

Antidepressant medications have been a profoundly helpful tool for managing or recovering from Major Depressive Disorder (MDD). Yet some patients prefer tapering off medications after symptoms decrease, due to unwanted side effects, expense, or other concerns. Other individuals have not experienced a substantial response even after trials of several different medications or prefer non-pharmacological approaches for other reasons.

Because some patients do not respond optimally to the first antidepressant, adding or switching to a different type of antidepressant is also a common scenario. Per the National Institute of Mental Health, even when some symptoms start to improve quickly, full therapeutic effects may take 4-8 weeks for many individuals.

Thankfully, medications are not the only effective depression treatment. Many MDD studies have reported that combining psychotherapy with antidepressant medication yields better outcomes than medication alone, especially for moderate to severe depression. Psychotherapy can help with initial symptom remission, maintaining progress, treatment satisfaction, and preventing relapses.

Therefore, evidence-based psychotherapies can be a powerful ally for recovery from depression, even for those already on medication. Research also indicates that the quality of the working relationship is more important to depression treatment outcomes than theoretical orientation by itself. It is vitally important to find a therapist with whom you are comfortable and can build a strong, trusting rapport.

Cognitive Behavioral therapies for depression have been particularly well studied. Generally speaking, these therapy approaches consider the impact of thinking and behaviors upon mood. Original Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) emphasized that automatic errors in thinking, such as catastrophizing or predominantly focusing on the negative aspects of situations, contribute to depressed mood.

CBT suggested that depressed individuals have disproportionately negative views of themselves, others, and their futures. Learning to correct thinking errors while also increasing constructive, rewarding behaviors are central components of CBT work. Well-implemented CBT has held up over decades as an effective depression treatment, albeit not the only one.

Today, many clinicians employ newer-generation cognitive behavioral therapies, which still consider depressive thought patterns. Instead of correcting faulty thoughts, however, the client’s focus is on changing their relationship to these thoughts.

Acceptance and Commitment Therapy

For example, Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) helps clients reduce attachment to unhelpful thinking by learning to observe thoughts as passing mental events rather than facts. Clients also work on acceptance of internal experiences and feelings. Acceptance does not mean that one must like all thoughts and emotions – only that their existence is observed and acknowledged.

Importantly, the next step is to take committed actions that are consistent with personal values, regardless of the current thoughts, internal sensations, and feelings. Rather than battling negative internal thoughts, the thoughts are noted, but energy is consciously redirected toward pursuing personally meaningful goals.

More specifically, six core processes are addressed by the therapist during the process of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy.

Work revolves around accepting the full range of thoughts and emotions, identifying and distancing from transient thoughts and emotions, increasing mindful awareness of the present moment, understanding one’s broader life context and the roles and meaning within it, identifying personal values, and taking committed action toward personally valued goals.

Throughout the process, clients are encouraged to observe patterns and track thoughts and behaviors that move them toward or away from desired goals. In this way, clients learn to improve psychological flexibility, giving them a healthier range of responses to life events and difficult emotions.

If you are struggling with symptoms of depression and these principles appeal to you, I encourage you to seek out a therapist trained in ACT. A skilled clinician can partner with you, using this evidence-based approach to treating depression and other mood disorders.

item.title: Overcoming Negative Thoughts from a Christian Counseling Perspective
item.description:
Negative thoughts and beliefs can create a loop, influencing your emotions and perceptions. Have you ever had a fleeting thought that changed how you felt? Perhaps you were happy, and a sudden thought occurred to you, and you felt down, sad, or even worthless.

Negative thoughts trigger our emotions and influence our actions in response. But you can overcome negative thoughts with a few psychological techniques.

Tips for Overcoming Negative Thoughts

Negative thoughts can sound true until you challenge them. Learning how to identify and “catch” your thoughts, manage them, and seek help when needed can shift your perspective and emotions.

The following are tips for overcoming negative thoughts. Try each one. They may feel uncomfortable at first, but as you continue to become more aware of the words you say to yourself, you will identify a pattern. A counselor can help you break the cycle.

“Catch” Your Thoughts

As a Holy Spirit-filled Christian, you have the divine weapons to “demolish arguments and every pretension that sets itself up against the knowledge of God, and we take captive every thought to make it obedient to Christ.” (2 Corinthians 10:6, NIV)

It is time to “catch” your own thoughts, taking them captive. Start paying close attention to the words you say aloud, the thoughts driving these words, and your actions. Take note of your emotions. If you notice you suddenly feel depressed or on edge, ask yourself what you were thinking about. Identify the negative thoughts that started the spiral.

Challenge Negative Thoughts

Not everything you think is true. Negative thoughts can seem true, and are often the result of black-and-white thinking (all-or-nothing), catastrophizing (this always happens), or mind-reading (you just know what someone else is thinking or saying).

Challenge these thoughts with the truth. Recognize the mind’s strategy. Ask yourself if what you think is really true.

Reframe Negative Thoughts

Once you have identified the negative thoughts and the strategy, reframe them around the truth. For example, you have no way of knowing what someone is thinking. Often, situations are not clear-cut, so all-or-nothing thinking will not get you anywhere. Consider leaving specific phrases out of your vocabulary for a while, such as saying, “This always happens to me!” or “I bet that happens.”

Work on reframing negative thoughts. Instead of thinking, “I bet she thought I was ignorant,” reframe the thought with, “I have no idea what she was thinking, but I did well, and I’m proud of myself.”

Journal Your Thoughts and Emotions to Reveal Patterns

Identifying and reframing negative thoughts might be easier if you consider journaling your thoughts and emotions to reveal thought and behavioral patterns. When you notice a negative thought, record it in your journal. Ask yourself if it is true and what thought strategy is behind it. Next, write out a reframing statement to counter the negative thought.

A counselor can help you identify patterns and create positive statements to say to yourself when the negative thoughts repeat.

When Negative Thoughts Seem Insurmountable

Sometimes, negative thoughts can seem insurmountable. They can convince us of lies and skew our perception of the truth. This misperception can lead to anxiety, depression, mood disorders, and other mental health conditions.

Contact our office today to schedule a session with a Christian counselor. The counselors in our network offer virtual and in-person sessions, and would love to help you overcome negative thoughts by arming you with the strategies to manage them for good. Speak to a representative today.

item.title: The Persistence of Mental Trauma: Why Avoidance Doesn’t Work
item.description:
The most current version of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual defines post-traumatic stress injury as experiencing or witnessing a singular or series of life-threatening events, or sustaining serious injury, or living through sexually violent offenses (American Psychiatric Association [APA], 2022). This is a good starting summary of trauma and stress.

The Science of Mental Trauma

There is certainly room for discussion about the awareness that, though much has been discovered in the world of scientific research, we may only be at the brink of knowledge when it comes to understanding human physicality and mental capacity. God has made the human body the resounding reflection of his own image and the pièce de resistance of his creation (Genesis 1-2).

There have been many wonderful discoveries through the course of history, but there is still so much yet to explore in understanding the human experiences of life that we may be exposed to. As humans, we experience things that are not clinically defined as trauma but that our bodies are telling us are equally traumatic or stressful.

God has created the body with an amazing feature where the brain sends the body multiple signals to identify that it is under significant stress or trauma and that healing is imminently needed.

The nervous system, and some other systems, give warning signals, just like a car provides a “check engine light,” that something needs emergent attention. Signals can include, but are not limited to:

  • Racing pulse
  • Nightmares
  • Environmental or sensory triggers that take a person in their mind back to the event
  • Irritability
  • Emotional numbness
  • Difficulty concentrating
  • The sudden urge to leave
  • A short temper because a person’s emotional bandwidth is reduced
  • An apathy toward people or things that normally bring joy
  • Difficulty resting or difficulty finding energy

Let’s call this a survival state and put it in context. If one day you show up to work and your boss yells at you in front of your coworkers, you might have a bad day, feel distressed, but chalk it up to your boss being out of line and hope it doesn’t happen again.

Let’s say it happens three weeks in a row. At the second occurrence, your body will start preparing itself to interact with your boss in anticipation of the possibility of them yelling at you again. Your body might tense.

Symptoms of Mental Trauma

The night before work, your sleep is off; you hide from your boss to reduce the possibility you might interact with them; you are irritable with your kids that morning as you dread going into work. The body is operating under stress and already working in a survival state.

For the sake of this discussion, while the situation was not life-threatening, it was stressful. It could be argued that identifying something as traumatic or stressful should first be assessed from the standpoint of how the body is responding, versus what exactly has occurred.

For example, chronic moving for a child can send the same physical and mental signals of stress as a military member returning from a difficult deployment, or a teenager facing the daily underhanded negative comments of a peer (Rachel E. Siciliano et al., 2022).

A state of survival is intended to be short-term, a length of time which is unique to every person. In some instances, this is a helpful physical mechanism where the rush of adrenaline keeps a person alive or provides the ability to respond to extreme hardship. The body can endure and heal from extreme hardship, but a chronic state of survival has profound effects on physical and mental functioning (von Majewski et al, 2023).

This is due to the science of how a physical and emotional state of readiness is inherently uncomfortable, requiring significant amounts of physical energy to sustain. Recall the side effects of trauma and stress above and note that what is predominantly impacted are physical and emotional outputs.

For example, a warning sign of unmanaged chronic trauma or stress might be constant fatigue or a sudden drop in energy levels throughout the day, where the body is informing you that it needs some type of rest and recovery or additional nutrition (Pivac, N. et al., 2023). It is natural, in fact wonderful, that God created a mechanism to motivate the body to find physiological and mental relief.

God and Mental Trauma

Furthermore, God gave us the Bible, His revelation of Himself as the answer to human suffering, which He reminded us we would encounter (John 16:33). Some directions He provided, knowing His creation perfectly, were to encourage us to meet with others, to develop meaningful relationships, and to seek counseling in relationships as part of counteracting and making sense of trauma and stress.

The catch twenty-two though, as mentioned before, is that trauma is inherently uncomfortable and often leads to avoidance. Processing trauma is frequently avoided, which doesn’t even address how circumstances often surrounding trauma and stress might impact the ability to respond to the inherently uncomfortable call to action.

To better understand processing trauma and make sense of suffering and tragedy, imagine that every person has a refrigerator. Every event experienced in a lifetime are items going into the fridge. Some items may have a longer shelf life than others. Either way, the fridge should be regularly cleared, cleaned, organized, maintained, and re-stocked for it to function optimally and preserve the food for the duration of its shelf life.

Imagine trauma is like buying a fish and placing it on an open plate in the fridge. At best, the shelf life of the fish may be 2-3 days. Every time the door to the fridge is opened, it is hard to miss how the open container of fish is beginning to affect every item in that fridge. The owner might even begin to eat only from the pantry to avoid opening the fridge door.

Avoiding trauma is like knowing there is raw fish in your fridge but closing the door and going on vacation for three weeks. Upon returning from vacation, a Franken-fish will have established territory in the fridge. Anyone else living in the same household with that fridge will also have to contend with the Franken-fish should they desire to even evaluate what their options are upon opening the door.

Family members may also begin to avoid, comment on, or act toward the fridge owner to resolve the concern of the Franken-fish. In other words, there is a shelf-life for managing trauma and stress. Long-term avoidance of trauma can seriously damage physical and emotional functioning and relationships.

What the Bible Has to Say

Now, as much as Jesus was about the business of fish in his ministry and might have had a fridge metaphor had they been around in that era, He was and is about other things. When reading Scripture, it can be helpful to pay close attention to the details, but it is also helpful to read with a ten-thousand-foot view. Paying close attention to the themes or rhythms of Scripture can show us how to set our own themes and rhythms in life.

When reading the gospels, particularly when Jesus began his ministry, there is a clear urgency to Jesus’ actions when healing others. In almost every, if not every, interaction where Jesus was approached by crowds or individuals for healing, He did not wait to heal. God is a healer and in the business of healing. There is also a theme of urgency and imminence throughout Scripture.

God urges people to wrestle with their understanding of who He is. Scripture is clear about the fact that no one knows the time or place or means of their passing. Life is depicted as vapor, a wind, the lifespan of a flower in the vast scheme of the universe. God is urging his creation to spend time figuring out who He is. God is also about relationships, where the essence of life is relationships. Humans are called to be in relationship with Him and others.

There are clear promises that, even if we feel the emotion of loneliness, we are not alone or are invited not to be alone. God is about rest (English Standard Version, 2001, Matthew 11:38-30), where God promises that when we are in relationship with Him, we find healing and peace at a soul level.

Our emotional healing is equally as important as our physical healing to God. God encourages us not to live with a spirit of fear, but to step out with confidence, trusting that as you face emotionally difficult things, God is with you in the process (English Standard Version, 2001,2Timothy 1:7).

Let’s put it all together. God is urging us not to wait to seek physical and emotional healing. With any measure of hope or courage, reach out, trusting that God will meet you as you wrestle with and make sense of trauma. Be confident that making sense of traumatic or stressful experiences, whether in a counseling setting or an informal setting, reflects some measure of courage, the act of facing something that might cause much fear or anxiety.

Next Steps

Processing trauma might also be the reflection of even a small amount of hope for healing, a relief from the side effects that often accompany trauma or stress. Remember that you are not required to do it alone. God is already there in the journey and has placed opportunities for counsel to help lead you. If you are feeling prompted, schedule an appointment with a counselor.

item.title: How to Help Children of Divorce: Advice from a Christian Counselor in Huntington Beach, CA
item.description:
Children of divorce may require more attention, encouragement, and support. Although the rate of divorce has been declining over the past two decades, at least 40% of first-time marriages end in divorce. The rate increases in subsequent marriages.

You can help your children find their footing, adapt, and thrive by working together, providing stability, teaching them how to regulate emotions, and leaning into God.

Tips for Helping Children of Divorce

Helping children of divorce cope with changes in a positive way can build emotional resilience and reassure them that they are still loved. You can establish these guideposts by providing a stable environment, acknowledging their thoughts and feelings, working to co-parent, and providing support from other sources. Uniting as a family to serve and worship in the church and community can teach children empathy as they learn about others.

Adjusting to a new normal is hard for both parents and children. Sometimes you need more guidance. Don’t be afraid of seeking professional help during this season. Christian counseling combines evidence-based psychological methods with faith-based principles, helping people work through hard seasons while drawing closer to God.

The following are several tips to help children of divorce adapt and thrive.

Build a stable environment

Children need stability. They need to know that they have a safe space to lay their head down at night and to be with a parent. During a divorce, so much can be up in the air, including living arrangements.

Often, parents start divorce proceedings and are unsure if they will sell their home and split the difference, if one parent will remain in the home, or if both parents need to move out of a rented place immediately.

In some circumstances, divorce is due to violent actions on the part of one parent, leaving the other parent to flee to safety. Trying to build a safe environment for your children helps to ease the tension and anxiety they feel.

If possible, make arrangements as soon as you become aware that divorce is impending. If it is an immediate separation due to divorce, confide in friends and family about a safe place to live temporarily while you find more secure housing. Inform your child that this is only temporary, but they will still be surrounded by love.

Remember that older children hurt too

We can get so bogged down with divorce proceedings that we forget that older children are not meant to shoulder the responsibility of carrying our emotions or raising younger siblings. Single parents tend to rely on older children for help.

Although older children should take on more responsibility as they grow, expecting them to act like adults or confiding in them as if they are adults will only cause feelings of resentment, bitterness, and anger to fester.

Older children hurt too, although they may be better at keeping it hidden. Your younger child may cry at night, but an older child may act out in other ways. They may have mood swings, lash out at younger siblings, develop behavioral issues in school, or suffer academically. Take the time to listen to your older child. Ask them questions about their thoughts and feelings, and acknowledge their insecurities.

Explain to them that a divorce is necessary after all avenues have been considered, but don’t go into the details of every argument between you and your spouse. Consider speaking to the teacher or counselor at your child’s school to inform them about a significant life event affecting your child that may impact their behavior or academics.

Try to coparent effectively

Coparenting can be tricky. First, you need to have a civil relationship with your ex. You do not need to be overly friendly, but you do need to work together for the sake of your children and maintain a positive relationship.

Children can sense the tension between parents during exchanges, and this can add to their anxiety. Try to keep the conversation focused on the children, updating the other parent about physical, emotional, and behavioral health, as well as academic performance.

If possible, try to attend extracurricular activities, especially games or performances. Even if you do not arrive together or sit together, your children will see that you both still support them in their endeavors. Decide on a reward system at your home and give your children your expectations of their behavior, but also be aware of your ex’s rules at their home.

Consider a mediator if you find it challenging to agree with the other parent. You may need someone else to help with exchanging the children temporarily until the newness of the separation and divorce is less emotionally charged and raw.

Keep schedules consistent

Children need routine to feel secure and stable in their environment and in relationships. Try to keep their daily and weekly schedules consistent, so they know what to expect.

For example, if you choose a coparenting schedule where the parents alternate weeks, keep that schedule. If something changes, inform your children about the change and whether it is temporary (for example, a parent has to travel for work and cannot take them that week) or permanent (the new schedule will be split into Sunday through Wednesday with Mom and Thursday through Sunday afternoon with Dad).

For teen children, consider asking them about what works better for them. It may be that walking home to Mom’s house after school is easier than waiting for the school bus to get dropped off at Dad’s home. Although you want to keep schedules consistent, both parents should remain flexible and be willing to change to make things smoother for the family.

Serve as a family

Family can be more than blood-related individuals. During and after a divorce is a good time to lean further into your church family.

Take your children to church and serve as a family in various ministries in and outside of the church. Your children learn to think about others, empathize, and see how they can be the hands and feet of Jesus to a hurting world. Schedule volunteer opportunities into your calendar and hang them up where the children can see.

Give them as much importance as you do doctor appointments or school. When children grow up doing good and showing Christ’s kindness to others in a family where religious beliefs are deemed necessary, the children are at a decreased risk of developing suicidal ideation or attempts, according to a study published in 2019 in Ethics Med Public Health.

Ask your church or local community center about volunteer opportunities. If you do not have a home church, ask friends and family about their churches or visit churches in your area that preach the Word of God and have a thriving children’s ministry.

Seek help as a family

Although it can be challenging, consider family counseling during or after divorce to help make coparenting smoother. Both parents can attend a few sessions with their children and work with a counselor to agree on schedules and expectations. After a divorce, as parents begin to date others and possibly remarry, family counseling can help in the introduction of new people into the children’s lives and blended family scenarios.

By seeking help as a family, you are reassuring your children that you want what is best for them and are willing to admit when you need help. Children learn life skills that will help them build emotional resilience.

Christian Counseling During and After Divorce

Children of divorce can struggle with the transition. Depending on the circumstances, these children may blame themselves, feel unseen, or even be angry. It’s okay to seek help from an unbiased third party at this time. A Christian counselor can help the whole family in the transition during and after divorce.

Contact our facility today to schedule a session with a counselor specializing in divorce and family counseling.

item.title: Learning How to Forgive Yourself When It Feels Impossible
item.description:
It’s easy to hold a grudge against someone who wronged you, but it can also be relatively easy to forgive them. Learning to forgive yourself can be more challenging. Forgiving usually goes something like this:

You replay the offensive action as it unfolded in real-time in your head with a judgmental eye. You speculate about motives and judge them in all their faults and frailties and talk it over with your best friend, who will assure you that you were not at fault (because that’s what best friends do). Eventually, forgiveness and acceptance can come through an apology, bringing restoration to the relationship and satisfaction to your soul.

But when you’re holding resentment against yourself, the act of forgiveness can be more complicated and the process less straightforward. Do you want to confess and regurgitate your transgressions with someone else? And when you’re fighting with yourself, a healing apology may not be forthcoming.

Why It’s Important to Forgive Yourself

Sometimes we’re easy on ourselves, like the time you justified popping a few grapes at the grocery store just to test them. There are other times when we are our own harshest judges. Our self-serving bias may allow us to take credit for our successes (of course they’re a result of my abilities). When it comes to our failures, we may blame those on external factors such as someone else’s actions or even bad luck.

But when we judge our actions with the ferociousness of a chef judging a microwave dinner, we forget that we should also show ourselves grace. Holding yourself to a high standard is commendable, but so is forgiving yourself when you fall short of those goals. After all, even those award-winning chefs have off days and come home to microwave a TV dinner.

We’re allowed to learn and grow and to try again and again without the constraints of self-criticism holding us back.

Viewing yourself through the lens of your mistakes can weigh you down, making even your victories and moments of peace a little less meaningful. When you forgive yourself, you can let go of that weighty guilt and relentless regret. This means you can stop carrying around the weight of your mistakes. Because you know what? God has already promised to forgive you.

Learning to Accept Forgiveness

As a follower of Christ, you know you are called to forgive others, but that same grace and compassion should be extended to yourself. God has already made a way for your forgiveness by sending His only Son to die for your sins. Now, you just have to accept that gift and release yourself from the harshness of your regret.

That process isn’t always easy. In fact, forgiving yourself can be even more difficult than forgiving others and is a deeply personal process. We’ve all been told to “let it go!” But letting go is easier said than done.

Support as You Forgive Yourself

Thankfully, you don’t have to walk the path alone. A Bible-believing therapist can serve as an invaluable ally in this sometimes-tumultuous process. Your therapist can help you break free from the constricting chains of guilt and point you back into the loving and compassionate arms of the Lord. They can also help you uncover the root of your feelings, reframe your thinking, and empower you to move forward through healing and hope, so you don’t stumble back into self-deprecation.

Forgiving yourself means seeing yourself through the lens of God’s everlasting love, not the foggy and scratched lens of sin and regret. God’s grace is much bigger than your failures and much more everlasting than your sins. Regardless of your past failures and mistakes, you can walk in confidence knowing that you are loved and forgiven. Let the therapists at our location help you find that forgiveness. Give our office a call today.

item.title: 7 Successful Aging Secrets of Happy People
item.description:
The phrase “successful aging” can be fraught with misunderstanding and lower self-esteem in geriatric populations. However, it aligns with positive psychology. This is focused on mental health factors that contribute to longevity and overall well-being. Research indicates that aging well (in healthful ways) correlates with aging happily.

In other words, happy people have discovered the secrets to successful aging by maintaining lifestyles that promote overall well-being. Here are seven factors that contribute to their wellness:

Happy people are healthy people

This one may seem obvious, but in many research studies, the people who were the healthiest as they aged were also the happiest. It may be that their outlook on life helped their mental health and physical well-being thrive, or that their positive attitudes and experiences contributed to their well-being.

One thing is true: Multiple researchers have placed at least some connection between health and happiness. We can make a similar connection from the Book of Proverbs in the Bible.

Proverbs 17 says, “A joyful heart is good medicine, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones.” (Proverbs 17:22, ESV) Another verse in Proverbs links joy to good health: “The light of the eyes rejoices the heart, and good news refreshes the bones.” (Proverbs 15:30, ESV) Focusing on one’s inner life is something everyone can do to take steps toward a life of joy and longevity.

Focus on positive memories

As humans age, we all have selective memories that stick with us (or don’t). Recent research shows that older segments of the population tend to focus on what they remember as good more than young or mid-life adults. This is good news for us as we age!

It shows that not only do we stand to remember more of the good we’ve experienced in life, but we can choose to fix our thoughts on those good, heartwarming memories, which helps us age with more joy. The cyclical effect of positive thought patterns is also echoed in the Bible.

Philippians 4 teaches that our propensity for thankfulness directly affects our peace, and that as we practice focusing on what is noble, excellent, and praiseworthy, our hearts will be at peace.

Finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable, if there is any excellence, if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things. What you have learned and received and heard and seen in me – practice these things, and the God of peace will be with you. – Philippians 4:8-9, ESV

Stay active

This isn’t a secret: most of us know that our activity levels, particularly as we get older, are an important factor in our overall health. However, research shows that the people who are happiest as they age are also those who maintain their commitment to physical fitness.

Whether it’s a 30-minute walk, a 20-minute strength training video, or a combination, choosing a routine you can maintain as you get older will not just improve your physical health but also your mental health. Physical activity promotes the functioning of your hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal (HPA), which reduces cortisol levels.

Research shows that elevated cortisol levels can contribute to anxiety, depression, and PTSD. So, physical exercise helps with successful aging and overall health.

Develop and maintain social connections

You’ve spent a lifetime learning how to make and keep friends, and while life transitions make it harder, this isn’t the time to hold onto a grudge. One study showed that conversations with friends every day were even more pleasant than interactions with marital partners. Friends tended to discuss less stressful topics. Friendship is also associated with an elevated mood.

According to several articles in Forbes magazine, friendships can change as you get older, and that’s okay. In fact, to expect them to stay the same, or not to make any new friends as you age, is unrealistic. Life transition, shifting interests, and widening support networks are all reasons that a friendship may not be what it once was. But many older adults maintain friendships throughout their lifetime.

Keys to that maintenance involve allowing the other person to change, being respectful, resolving conflicts, and continually learning new things together. Learning to make new friends is also valuable, particularly since friendships will be lost as you get older.

Successful aging benefits from having a variety of friend types. Once you retire, it will be more difficult to maintain workplace friendships simply because your season of life shifts. But it can be done, particularly if both people are committed to supporting each other. Outside of co-workers, you can make new friends by volunteering for a cause you enjoy, getting to know the other grandparents of your grandchildren, and looking to befriend someone younger than you.

Younger friends are a benefit that goes both ways. Your capacity to learn new things enlarges as you’re exposed to a younger subset of people, but you can also invest your wisdom into the lives of others who aren’t as far down their journey as you are. Leading others, formally through civic and church groups or informally, such as with a neighbor, is a fantastic way to broaden your relational base.

Consider seeing a therapist for your mental and emotional health

There’s quite a bit of research on subjective well-being and positive psychology, and it tells us that your positive emotions and attitude have a significant impact on your perceived happiness, especially as you age. One study found that how you evaluate your life based on satisfaction varies with attitude, interactions, emotional well-being, and resilience.

The positive side of aging successfully or happily depends on several factors surrounding emotional and mental health. A person’s perception of life and the joy and positivity they feel about it are directly connected to longevity. Essentially, if you’re struggling with anger, sadness, and unhealed wounds from others, it’s essential to see a mental health professional.

Remaining stuck in old patterns or negative emotions can detract from your years, but it can also make the remaining years seem worse than they actually are. Just like you would want to look at a fading photograph through glasses that are clean and clear, you’ll want to approach aging through a mentally and emotionally healthy lens.

You can do this by seeing a licensed counselor regularly. Our offices are equipped with trained therapists who can guide you through this season. When a friend passes away or a family member hurts your feelings or tries to make decisions for you, it’s important to seek wise counsel so you know how to view yourself and those around you. Working through old hurts or present grievances can give you that jump-start.

Pursue new hobbies and activities

While studies are ongoing, preliminary research suggests that learning a new skill like photography, quilting, or creative activities like music and art may benefit your cognitive skills. Unlike recommended memory games, creative activities show promise in boosting more than working memory. They also contribute to a person’s emotional and mental wellness routine by calming agitation and relieving stress.

If you can double the benefit, why not? Consider enrolling in your local community center’s adult classes and workshops to gain the most benefit. You’ll get to meet new people and add to your social network, too.

Get the optimal amount of sleep

Multiple studies tout the benefits of sleep for all ages, but for successful aging, it’s even more imperative to get adequate shut-eye. Not only does sleep affect metabolic and endocrine functioning, but it also influences hormonal levels, which correlate with a person’s mood.

If you’re going for a more joyful aging process, sleep is like the umbrella for all the other choices you make. As you get older, conditions such as sleep apnea may make restful, restorative sleep more difficult. Speak with your clinician to learn about how best to treat underlying conditions.

Successful aging can bring you vitality and discourage ageism in your local community, which ripples down to younger generations. If you’d like a guide to walk you through some of these shifts, contact one of our offices. We can help you find a therapist who specializes in working with older adults.

item.title: What You Should Know About Chronic Anxiety
item.description:
Worry, anxiety, and fear are hallmarks of chronic anxiety. People with chronic anxiety feel stuck in the fight or flight response (or the freeze response). They become overwhelmed and anxious disproportionately to the situation. This fear can lead to panic attacks and other conditions.

Do you have chronic anxiety? Professional treatment is available.

What is chronic anxiety?

Chronic anxiety is fear-based worry that surfaces even without a conscious trigger. It is anxiety that runs under the surface. When anxiety is not treated, it can lead to physical, emotional, and mental issues. Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is a mental condition that addresses chronic anxiety. If you feel that you cannot relax, always feel “on edge,” or have constant muscle tension, you may have chronic anxiety.

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), as many as 301 million people suffer from an anxiety disorder (2019). Forbes estimates this number to have risen to over 314 million people in 2023.

If you suspect that you have chronic anxiety, you are not alone. However, anxiety disorders are manageable.

What is the difference between chronic anxiety and panic attacks?

Chronic anxiety is the underlying tension you may feel even when you are not around a trigger. Your thoughts might race about your worries and fears. The anxiety may keep you awake at night.

A panic attack comes on suddenly. An episode can happen during a stressful event or at the thought of one. At times, you may experience a panic attack without any warning and no conscious thoughts about a trigger.

Symptoms of a panic attack include:

  • Shortness of breath
  • Dizziness, lightheadedness, or feeling faint
  • Chest tightness or pressure
  • Increase in blood pressure
  • Rapid heart rate
  • Chills or hot flashes
  • Trouble swallowing or feeling suffocated
  • Feelings of doom or dread
  • Fear of dying or losing control

You may experience the symptoms of a panic attack for up to 30 minutes after the start. However, specific symptoms, such as rapid heart rate and increased blood pressure, may last a few hours.

Check with your physician after a panic attack to rule out other conditions, as the symptoms of a panic attack can mimic other problems.

What is the treatment for chronic anxiety?

One of the most effective treatments for chronic anxiety is psychotherapy (talk therapy). You can schedule a session with a counselor for one-on-one, couples, family, or group sessions. Depending on your triggers, your counselor may recommend a combination of different types of sessions.

You can also choose between in-person and virtual sessions. As well as incorporating God’s word and promises such as reframing our thoughts and renewing our minds.

Do not conformed to this world [any longer with its superficial values and customs], but be transformed and progressive led changed [as you mature spiritually] by the renewing of your mind [focusing on godly values and ethical attitudes], so that you may prove [for yourselves] what the will of God is, that which is good and acceptable and perfect [in his plan and purpose for you]. – Romans 12:2, AMP

What you can do to reduce chronic anxiety

Counseling is an effective treatment strategy for chronic anxiety, but lifestyle tweaks can help you to manage symptoms better. You were made for so much more than being bound in fear and worry.

Read through the following list of tips and choose a few to try this week.

Exercise

Exercise enhances your well-being by triggering the brain to release a cascade of feel-good chemicals. This release works like a natural anti-depressant and pain reliever. Have you ever noticed how good you feel after a sweaty workout? That is the brain’s reward system for moving the body.

Check with your doctor before starting a new exercise regimen. Once cleared, aim for at least thirty minutes several days per week to reap the physical and mental benefits.

Journaling

The act of journaling can be enough to relieve stress and tension regarding some issues. Instead of lying awake in bed at night, thinking about problems, consider writing about what is bothering you. You can also try this exercise first thing in the morning. You may see that pouring your worries out onto the page is an effective strategy for removing the topics from the forefront of your mind.

You can keep your journal private or share it with your counselor. You may find that solutions work themselves out after you have written the problem down and can see it more objectively. The act of journaling also helps you to distance yourself from a situation.

Socializing

Anxiety lies to us. It whispers negative thoughts and leaves us isolated. Getting out with a friend for lunch or coffee may be just what the doctor ordered. Socializing with others allows us to listen to what is happening in our friends’ lives and share a few laughs.

When was the last time that you invited friends out for an event? Are there any local events that would be more fun with friends? Invite those closest to you out for dinner or a coffee shop run. Not only is socializing good for your soul, but it may be what a friend needs now.

Not forsaking our meeting together [as believers for worship and instructions], as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more [faithfully] as you see the day [of Christ’s return] approaching. – Hebrews 10:25, AMP

Deep breathing

There seems to be a great deal of social media coverage regarding deep breathing. Everyone seems to be practicing it, but why? Is the practice of deep breathing to relieve chronic anxiety effective? Deep breathing triggers the body’s natural processes for rest.

Deep breathing helps to calm the sympathetic nervous system and activates the parasympathetic nervous system (PNS). The PNS manages the body’s response to rest. After a stressful day or event, the PNS begins the process of relaxing your nerves and state of mind. Your heart rate decreases, as does your blood pressure. Muscle tension begins to dissipate. Your body “resets” itself.

Reading

Reading, particularly fiction, is a form of escapism. It allows you to immerse yourself into a story and temporarily “forget” your worry or fear. When you read a novel, your mind focuses on the story. Your imagination comes to life. The act of reading a story decreases anxiety.

If it has been a while since you have taken the time to read a novel, ask for suggestions from your friends, family, coworkers, and library staff. More people read across several genres, so do not feel awkward if you want to read a Young Adult book as an adult. Find stories that will take you on an adventure. You may want to read before bed or keep your book (a reading app is excellent for eBooks) with you to take little reading breaks throughout the day.

Praying

Praying should not be the last resort when we feel stressed or worried, yet many times it is. Seek God when you feel your anxiety level rising or experiencing a panic attack. You can pray silently or out loud. Thank God for your blessings, and ask Him to forgive you for anything you have said or done that was not in line with His will. God convicts us, but His Spirit does not condemn us as Christians.

There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit. – Romans 8:1, NKJV

As you pray, believe that God loves and cares for you and works things out for your good and His purpose. Knowing that the One who created the heavens and the earth and everything we see and hear loves and cares enough for us to sacrifice His only Son so that we can have closer access to Him reminds us that we are important to God.

And, putting on the whole armor of God, did you know that God warns us that we would face adversities, and trials, and have many enemies? Those enemies are not flesh but spiritual warfare to steal, kill, and destroy us.

In treatment, we will learn many coping skills to help relax and reduce the intensity of those anxious feelings. God bestowed us with the best coping skills, found in the book of Ephesians. The armor of God includes the belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, the gospel of peace, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, the sword of the Spirit, and prayer.

Speak up

Chronic anxiety can diminish your quality of life. Answer the following questions to determine if anxiety and worry are interfering with your daily activities:

  • Do you sweat excessively when confronted by a trigger?
  • Does your heart rate increase with thoughts of a trigger?
  • Do you avoid situations, locations, or people?
  • Do you experience panic attack symptoms?
  • Do you experience chronic anxiety symptoms and feelings of dread or doom?
  • Do you feel like this anxiety will last forever?

Chronic anxiety is treatable; we can help you overcome worry, fear, and dread. Contact our office today to schedule an appointment with a counselor specializing in chronic anxiety. Let us help you resume your daily life without fear and with the help of our Yahweh-Rapha – The Lord that Heals (Exodus 15:26).
